rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī argues that spectacular gifts do not prove spiritual rank: Iblīs, Balaam, and Israelite scholars received knowledge or ascetic distinction yet fell through pride in it.
rows.anchor: ظاهر الكرامات في حق إبليس وفي حق بلعام كان عظيما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A gift is other than its giver; delighting in a gift makes the recipient spiritually poor, while seeing only the Giver in gifts and creation marks genuine arrival.
rows.anchor: الكرامة غير المكرم وكل ما هو غير المكرم فهو ذليل

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Abraham's reply, “As for You, no,” illustrates refusing to rely on a poor or deficient thing; reliance on the Real alone is freedom.
rows.anchor: قال الخليل صلوات الله عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Self-admiration is characteristic of Iblīs and Pharaoh; false claimants to prophethood or divinity seek self-aggrandizement and feed vanity.
rows.anchor: الافتخار بالنفس وبصفاتها من صفات إبليس وفرعون

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet listed three destructive traits, ending with a person's self-admiration.
rows.anchor: قال عليه السلام : ( ثلاث مهلكات ، وختمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After receiving a great gift, Moses was directed to serve the Giver and remain grateful, not to rejoice in the gift itself.
rows.anchor: فلما أعطاه الله العطية الكبرى أمره بالاشتغال بخدمة المعطى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet chose to be a servant-prophet rather than a prophet-king; servanthood lets him glory in his Lord rather than in subjects.
rows.anchor: ترك ذلك الملك واختار العبودية لأنه إذا كان عبدا

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: The tashahhud wording transmitted by Ibn Masʿūd calls Muḥammad God's servant and messenger, underscoring the honor of servanthood.
rows.anchor: رواها ابن مسعود ( وأشهد أن محمدا عبده ورسوله )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One who loves the Lord should not rejoice in anything other than Him; rejoicing in gifts reveals love of self, the greatest idol, which Rāzī calls more dangerous than worshipping images.
rows.anchor: فمن أحب المولى لم يفرح بغير المولى ولم يستأنس بغير المولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's promise of an opening and provision is tied to God-consciousness and reliance, so these states do not arise without them.
rows.anchor: ومن يتق الله يجعل له مخرجا * ويرزقه

rows.speaker: الأستاذ أبو بكر بن فورك
rows.claim: Ibn Fūrak holds that a saint cannot know that he is a saint.
rows.anchor: قال الأستاذ أبو بكر بن فورك لا يجوز

rows.speaker: الأستاذ أبو علي الدقاق
rows.claim: Al-Daqqāq, followed by his student al-Qushayrī, holds that a saint may know his own sainthood.
rows.anchor: قال الأستاذ أبو علي الدقاق وتلميذه أبو القاسم القشيري يجوز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opponents argue that certainty of sainthood would grant security, but security and despair are forbidden; security presumes divine incapacity and despair presumes miserliness, both unbelief.
rows.anchor: الأمن لا يحصل إلا عند اعتقاد العجز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second argument says abundant obedience cannot make one secure when God's overpowering might remains greater.
rows.anchor: أن الطاعات وإن كثرت إلا أن قهر الحق أعظم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third argument says security removes servanthood and fear, whereas God's sincere servants combine hope and awe.
rows.anchor: أن الأمن يقتضي زوال العبودية وترك الخدمة والعبودية يوجب العداوة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One gloss takes their hope and fear as hope for God's reward and fear of His punishment.
rows.anchor: رغبا في ثوابنا / ورهبا من عقابنا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another gloss takes their hope as hope for God's bounty and their fear as fear of His justice.
rows.anchor: رغبا في فضلنا ، ورهبا من عدلنا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further gloss takes their hope as longing for union with God and their fear as fear of separation.
rows.anchor: رغبا في وصالنا ، ورهبا من فراقنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī prefers the more encompassing reading: they hope in God and fear God.
rows.anchor: والأحسن أن يقال رغبا فينا ، ورهبا منا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A saint cannot infer divine love from present obedience or enmity from present sin: God's eternal, uncaused love and enmity are hidden, and finite new acts cannot determine them.
rows.anchor: محبة الحق وعداوته سران لا يطلع عليهما أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sainthood and final reward depend on one's ending, not the start or present course of life; a late convert may be saved and a late apostate condemned, so no one knows the ending.
rows.anchor: العبرة بالخاتمة لا بأول العمل

rows.speaker: أبو علي الدقاق والقشيري
rows.claim: Those allowing self-knowledge say sainthood has two pillars: outward obedience to the law and inward absorption in the light of spiritual reality, recognizable through joy in obedience and intimacy with remembrance.
rows.anchor: أما الذين قالوا إن الولي قد يعرف كونه وليا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī rejects confident self-certification: the matter is obscure and hard to judge, experience is perilous, certainty is conceit, and veils separate people from divine reality.
rows.anchor: والقضاء عسر ، والتجربة خطر ، والجزم غرور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening says God recounts the youths' true account: they were a group of young men who believed in God.
rows.anchor: نحن نقص عليك نبأهم بالحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We strengthened their hearts” means God inspired patience and made them steadfast.
rows.anchor: أي ألهمناها الصبر وثبتناها

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says they were city notables who gathered outside without arranging it, and one disclosed that he felt their Lord was Lord of the heavens and earth.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد كانوا عظماء مدينتهم فخرجوا فاجتمعوا وراء المدينة من غير ميعاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second account says they stood before the tyrant Daqyānūs, confessed God as Lord of the heavens and earth, and were divinely strengthened to resist him and renounce partners.
rows.anchor: وقالوا : ربنا رب السموات والأرض

rows.speaker: عطاء ومقاتل
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ and Muqātil say they made the declaration on waking, but Rāzī finds this unlikely because the account is introduced afterward as a new narration.
rows.anchor: وهو قول عطاء ومقاتل أنهم قالوا ذلك عند قيامهم من النوم وهذا بعيد

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ explains shataṭ as going beyond the limit; its root imagery is distance, so it means straying far from truth, and it functions as a cognate accusative.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء يقال قد أشط في السوم إذ جاوز الحد

rows.speaker: الزجاج وغيره
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj and others also recognize shatta or ashatta for exceeding the limit.
rows.anchor: وحكى الزجاج وغيره شط الرجل وأشط إذا جاوز الحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “These our people” refers to the youths' contemporaries under Daqyānūs who worshipped idols; they challenge them to produce clear proof for that worship.
rows.anchor: هذا من قول أصحاب الكهف ويعنون الذين كانوا في زمان دقيانوس عبدوا الأصنام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some use the verse's appeal to absent proof to argue from lack of evidence to nonexistence; Rāzī calls that inference a strong method.
rows.anchor: فثبت أن الاستدلال بعدم الدليل على عدم المدلول طريقة قوية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asserting partners for God without evidence is slander and injustice, and the verse is a major proof against blind imitation.
rows.anchor: وهذا من أعظم الدلائل على فساد القول بالتقليد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The youths tell one another that withdrawing from the people and their objects of worship leaves their worship of God intact; they should make the cave their refuge.
rows.anchor: اعتزلتم الشيء الذي يعبدونه إلا الله فإنكم لم تعتزلوا عبادة الله

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ treats the cave command as the answer to idhā, like “when you do this, then do that”; it means go there and make it your abode.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء هو جواب إذ كما تقول إذ فعلت كذا فافعل كذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will spread His mercy over them and prepare ease in their affairs.
rows.anchor: أي يبسطها عليكم

rows.speaker: نافع وابن عامر وعاصم
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, and ʿĀṣim in one transmission read marfaq with fatḥa on mīm and kasra on fāʾ; the others use kasra on mīm and fatḥa on fāʾ.
rows.anchor: قرأن افع وابن عامر وعاصم في رواية مرفقا بفتح الميم وكسر الفاء

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ regards both marfaq pronunciations as dialect forms derived from irtifāq.
rows.anchor: وهما لغتان واشتقاقهما من الإرتفاق

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī accepts only the kasra-on-mīm reading for the body's elbow, while al-Farrāʾ accepts it for both the elbow and an affair.
rows.anchor: وكان الكسائي ينكر في مرفق الإنسان الذي في اليد إلا كسر الميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says both forms are dialects, with fatḥa more regular by analogy and kasra more common; marfaq can mean a means of support.
rows.anchor: وقيل هما لغتان إلا أن الفتح أقيس والكسر أكثر

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir reads tazawwar with a still zāy and doubled rāʾ, like taḥmar.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عامر تزور ساكنة الزاي

rows.speaker: عاصم وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī read tazāwar with an alif and lightening; the remaining readers double it. The readings all mean to incline.
rows.anchor: قرأ عاصم وحمزة والكسائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doubled form comes from tat-zāwar with assimilation, the light form is a reciprocal form from zawr, and tazawwar derives from izwirār.
rows.anchor: وأما التشديد فأصله تتزاور سكنت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You see the sun” addresses a hypothetical observer; it means that were the addressee to see it, the sun would incline from the cave.
rows.anchor: أن من خوطب بهذا يرى هذا المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhāt al-yamīn means the right-hand direction; dhāt, the feminine of dhū, stands in place of the noun it qualifies.
rows.anchor: وأصله أن ذات صفة أقيمت مقام الموصوف

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī says qaraḍtu al-makān means to turn aside from a place.
rows.anchor: قال الكسائي قرضت المكان أي عدلت عنه

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda gives qarḍ several senses including cutting across, so the sun passes away from their heads toward the north.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة القرض في أشياء فمنها القطع

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: One interpretation says the cave opening faced north, keeping direct sunlight out while pleasant air entered and prevented decay or damage to the youths' bodies.
rows.anchor: أن باب ذلك الكهف كان مفتوحا إلى جانب الشمال فإذا طلعت الشمس كانت على يمين الكهف

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj argues that God miraculously prevented sunlight from reaching them: the ordinary north-facing-cave account would not itself be a sign.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول الزجاج واحتج على صحته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They lay in a spacious part of the cave where air and cool breezes could reach them; fajwa means an open, roomy space.
rows.anchor: والفجوة متسع في مكان

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda gives fajawāt as the plural of fajwa and cites a report about moving briskly when finding open space.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة وجمعها فجوات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For those accepting divine prevention of sunlight, “that” refers to the sun's deviation; for others it means God's long protection of them in the cave.
rows.anchor: قالوا المراد من قوله ذلك أي ذلك التزاور والميل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their turn from unbelief to faith, like their bodily preservation, came by God's aid; the guided youths contrast with Daqyānūs and his unbelieving followers, and the verse raises known debates on predestination.
rows.anchor: فكذلك رجوعهم أولا عن الكفر ورغبتهم في الإيمان كان بإعانة الله ولطفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As with “you see the sun,” the wording means that if one saw the sleepers one would think they were awake.
rows.anchor: أي لو رأيتهم لحسبتهم { أيقاظا }

rows.speaker: الأخفش وأبو عبيدة والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash, Abū ʿUbayda, and al-Zajjāj say ayqāẓ is the plural of yaqiz or yaqẓān; a verse by Ruʾba illustrates the word.
rows.anchor: وهو جمع يقظ ويقظان قاله الأخفش وأبو عبيدة والزجاج

rows.speaker: رؤبة
rows.claim: Ruʾba's line uses ayqāẓ for awake people: “they found their brothers awake.”
rows.anchor: وأنشدوا لرؤبة : ووجدوا إخوانهم أيقاظا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ruqūd means sleeping; it is a verbal noun used adjectivally for a plural, and Rāzī rejects deriving it as the plural of rāqid because that pattern is unattested for active participles.
rows.anchor: وهم رقود أي نائمون وهو مصدر سمي المفعول به

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī says their open eyes made them appear awake.
rows.anchor: لأن أعينهم مفتحة وهم نيام

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says their repeated turning made them look awake, as the following clause explains.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج لكثرة تقلبهم يظن أنهم أيقاظ

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A report from Abū Hurayra says they were turned onto their sides twice each year.
rows.anchor: فعن أبي هريرة رضي الله عنه أن لهم في كل عام تقليبتين

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says they remained on their right sides for nine years, then on their left sides for nine years.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد يمكثون على أيمانهم تسع سنين ثم يقلبون على شمائلهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says they were turned only once, on the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقيل لهم تقليبة واحدة في يوم عاشوراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī rejects these precise schedules: reason cannot determine them, the Qurʾān does not specify them, and no sound report establishes them.
rows.anchor: هذه التقديرات لا سبيل للعقل إليها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says turning them prevented the earth from eating their flesh or wearing them away.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما فائدة تقليبهم لئلا تأكل الأرض لحومهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī finds that rationale strange: the God who kept them alive for over three hundred years could preserve their bodies without turning them.
rows.anchor: لما قدر على أن يمسك حياتهم مدة ثلثمائة سنة وأكثر فلم لا يقدر على حفظ أجسادهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhāt is adverbial here, meaning on the side or in the direction of the right or left, as in the previous verse.
rows.anchor: منصوبة على الظرف لأن المعنى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وأكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and most commentators say the youths fled by night and a shepherd's dog followed them in their faith.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس وأكثر المفسرين قالوا إنهم هربوا ليلا من ملكهم

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb says a dog repeatedly barked after them; it then declared love for God's beloved and offered to guard them.
rows.anchor: وقال كعب مروا بكلب فنبح عليهم فطردوه

rows.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr says the dog was their hunting dog.
rows.anchor: وقال عبيد بن عمير كان ذلك كلب صيدهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dog's outstretched forelegs lay flat on the ground, like the posture the Prophet prohibited in prayer when he likened it to a lion's sprawl.
rows.anchor: أنه نهى عن افتراش السبع

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says waṣīd is the forecourt or entrance of a house or dwelling and gives its plurals.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج الوصيد فناء البيت وفناء الدار وجمعه وصائد ووصد

rows.speaker: يونس والأخفش والفراء
rows.claim: Yūnus, al-Akhfash, and al-Farrāʾ treat waṣīd and aṣīd as dialect variants, like wakāf and ikāf.
rows.anchor: وقال يونس والأخفش والفراء الوصيد والأصيد لغتان مثل الوكاف والإكاف

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says waṣīd means the door; the cave had no actual door or threshold, so the dog occupied the threshold's position.
rows.anchor: الباب والكهف لا يكون له باب ولا عتبة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj explains iṭṭalaʿta ʿalayhim as looking down on them or seeing them from above.
rows.anchor: يقال اطلعت عليهم أي أشرفت عليهم

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says farāran is a cognate accusative because wallayta means “you fled.”
rows.anchor: منصوب على المصدر لأن معنى وليت منهم فررت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some explain the terror by their long hair and nails and open eyes while asleep; another view says God made anyone who saw them panic, which Rāzī considers sounder while leaving the precise cause to God.
rows.anchor: فالله أعلم به . وهذا هو الأصح

rows.speaker: نافع وابن كثير
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ and Ibn Kathīr read lamuʾiʾt with a doubled lām; the rest lighten it, and one transmission from Ibn Kathīr also lightens it. The senses are alike, with doubling more emphatic.
rows.anchor: قرأ نافع وابن كثير لملئت بتشديد اللام والهمزة والباقون بتخفيف اللام

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash says the light reading is more idiomatic Arabic; poetic usage supports it, though the doubled form is also attested.
rows.anchor: قال الأخفش الخفيفة أجود في كلام العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Several poetic lines attest the light reading of “filled me with terror,” while a line by al-Mukhabbal al-Saʿdī attests the doubled form.
rows.anchor: وأنشدوا للمخبل السعدي

rows.speaker: ابن عامر والكسائي
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir and al-Kisāʾī pronounce the ʿayn of ruʿban with ḍamma throughout the Qurʾān; the other readers use sukūn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر والكسائي رعبا بضم العين في جميع القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their awakening was like revival from sleep resembling death; they had remained alive without food or drink, and were turned over, so God revived them to question one another about their stay.
rows.anchor: فكذلك بعثناهم أي أحييناهم من تلك النومة التي تشبه الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their questioning can itself be an intended purpose: it disclosed extraordinary aspects of God's power, and such disclosure is desirable for its own sake.
rows.anchor: وذلك الانكشاف أمر مطلوب لذاته

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Commentators say they entered the cave in the morning and awoke near day's end, explaining why they guessed a day or part of one.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون إنهم دخلوا الكهف غدوة وبعثهم الله في آخر النهار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the speaker who returned the duration to God as their leader Yamlikhā, who inferred from their changed hair, nails, and faces that much time had passed.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس هو رئيسهم يمليخا رد علم ذلك إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وحمزة وأبو بكر عن عاصم
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza, and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim read wariqikum with sukūn on rāʾ and fatḥa on wāw; Ibn Kathīr reads kasra on rāʾ and assimilates qāf into kāf.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو وحمزة وأبو بكر عن عاصم بورقكم ساكنة الراء مفتوحة الواو

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Muḥayṣin's reading combines kasra on wāw with sukūn on rāʾ and assimilation, which Rāzī rejects because it creates two consecutive sukūns.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن محيصن أنه كسر الواو وأسكن الراء وأدغم القاف في الكاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wariq means silver, coined or uncoined; a report about ʿArfaja using a silver nose supports the uncoined sense, and several vowel forms are attested.
rows.anchor: والورق اسم للفضة سواء كانت مضروبة أم لا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ lists the forms waraqu, warqu, and wariqu, and calls kasra on wāw the least good form.
rows.anchor: ذكره الفراء والزجاج قال الفراء وكسر الواو أردؤها

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azharī says riqqa, another word for silver, derives from wariq through the pattern of ṣila and ʿida.
rows.anchor: قال الأزهري أصله ورق مثل صلة وعدة

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Commentators say the youths carried coins bearing the image of the king of their time and that their city was what is now called Tarsus.
rows.anchor: كانت معهم دراهم عليها صورة الملك الذي كان في زمانهم يعني بالمدينة التي يقال لها اليوم طرسوس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The episode shows that taking steps to secure food is important and does not negate reliance on God.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية تدل على أن السعي في إمساك الزاد أمر مهم مشروع وأنه لا يبطل التوكل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the purest food as lawful slaughter, since most inhabitants were Magians, though some secretly believed.
rows.anchor: يريد ما حل من الذبائح لأن عامة أهل بلدهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says they sought food farthest from the tyrant's injustice; other glosses understand the phrase as tastiest or cheapest.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد : كان ملكهم ظالما

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj parses ayyuhā as subject, azkā as its predicate, and ṭaʿāman as a specification.
rows.anchor: رفع بالابتداء ، و { أزكى } خبره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emissary should act discreetly while entering the city and buying food, and tell nobody where the youths are.
rows.anchor: أي يكون ذلك في سر وكتمان يعني دخول المدينة وشراء الطعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the townspeople discover or overpower them, they may stone them to death or force them back into their religion, leaving them no success if they return to unbelief.
rows.anchor: أي يطلعوا ويشرفوا على مكانكم أو على أنفسكم

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says rajm here means killing by stoning; rajm often denotes killing in revelation and is the worst kind of death.
rows.anchor: أي يقتلوكم بالرجم ، والرجم أخبث أنواع القتل

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj takes idhā abadan as implying a condition: if they return to the townspeople's religion, they will never prosper.
rows.anchor: قوله : { إذا أبدا } يدل على الشرط

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: The judge says an escaping believer faces the worst outcomes: bodily destruction by a vile death or religious destruction by a return to unbelief.
rows.anchor: ما على المؤمن الفار بدينه أعظم من هذين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though coercion might justify outwardly professing unbelief, Rāzī says prolonged forced profession could incline the heart until the person becomes an unbeliever inwardly, which explains their fear.
rows.anchor: أليس أنهم لو أكرهوا على الكفر حتى إنهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As with their guidance and awakening, God made others discover their state because it carried evident lessons; athartu means to discover or learn something, from stumbling upon it and then recognizing it.
rows.anchor: أي أطلعنا غيرهم على أحوالهم يقال عثرت على كذا أي علمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says their unusually long hair and nails and altered facial appearance revealed that an extraordinary length of time had passed.
rows.anchor: أنه طالت شعورهم وأظفارهم طولا مخالفا للعادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says the emissary's old coins were recognized by a seller as long obsolete; the king learned the man had fled Daqyānūs the day before and concluded God had revived him.
rows.anchor: هذه النقود غير موجودة في هذا اليوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God revealed the youths so people would know His promise of resurrection is true; their awakening after a long sleep demonstrates bodily resurrection.
rows.anchor: أطلعنا القوم على أحوالهم ليعلم القوم أن وعد الله حق بالبعث والحشر والنشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says the king denied resurrection but was fair-minded; another says people disputed whether body and soul or only the soul would be raised, and the king prayed for a sign that settled the issue.
rows.anchor: روى أن ملك ذلك الوقت كان ممن ينكر البعث إلا أنه كان مع كفرة منصفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “while they were disputing among themselves” attaches to God making the people discover the youths, at the time of their dispute.
rows.anchor: متعلق باعثرنا أي أعثرناهم عليهم حين يتنازعون بينهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their dispute may have concerned resurrection: believers used God's preservation of the bodies for 309 years as proof that He can raise bodies after death.
rows.anchor: فالقائلون به استدلوا بهذه الواقعة على صحته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the townspeople saw them, God may have returned the youths to the cave and caused their death; people then disagreed whether they slept again or had now died.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون بل الآن ماتوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some proposed sealing the cave so no one could enter, while others proposed building a mosque; this second proposal suggests they knew God, worship, and prayer.
rows.anchor: الأولى أن يسد باب الكهف لئلا يدخل عليهم أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says unbelievers claimed the sleepers followed their religion and wanted a monument, while Muslims said they followed theirs and proposed a mosque.
rows.anchor: القول الرابع : أن الكفار قالوا : إنهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reported disputes concerned how long the youths stayed and their number and names.
rows.anchor: والقول الخامس : أنهم تنازعوا في قدر مكثهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Their Lord knows best” may be the disputants' admission after failing to establish their names, circumstances, or duration, or it may be God's own correction of their speculation.
rows.anchor: أنه من كلام المتنازعين كأنهم لما تذاكروا أمرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who prevailed over the matter are variously identified as the Muslim king, the sleepers' relatives, or the town's leaders.
rows.anchor: قيل المراد به الملك المسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They proposed a mosque where people could worship God and preserve the youths' traces.
rows.anchor: نعبد الله فيه ونستبقي آثار أصحاب الكهف بسبب ذلك المسجد

rows.speaker: السيد والعاقب
rows.claim: The Christian visitors from Najrān report competing counts: Sayyid, a Jacobite, says three youths and a dog; al-ʿĀqib, a Nestorian, says five and a dog; Muslims say seven and a dog.
rows.anchor: السيد والعاقب وأصحابهما من أهل نجران كانوا عند النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī argues that seven plus the dog is correct: the waw before “eighth” marks a firmly established description; the first two counts are explicitly called conjecture, while this count is treated differently.
rows.anchor: قال أكثر المفسرين هذا الأخير هو الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The waw can enter a clause describing an indefinite noun or modifying a definite noun and emphasize that the stated quality is firmly established.
rows.anchor: هي الواو التي تدخل على الجملة الواقعة صفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the Qurʾān specifically adds this waw, Rāzī says it must convey an extra benefit, identifying this count as accepted rather than conjectural.
rows.anchor: خص هذا الموضع بهذا الحرف الزائد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the first two counts “conjecture” implies that the remaining count differs from them and is not baseless guessing.
rows.anchor: وتخصيص الشيء بالوصف يدل على أن الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The following statement that only a few know their number distinguishes the seven-count from the first two guesses and implies its greater accuracy.
rows.anchor: ما يعلمهم إلا قليل

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: ʿAlī says the seven were Yamlikhā, Maksalmīnā, Maslathīnā, Marnūs, Dabarnūs, Sādanūs, and the shepherd, and names the dog Quṭmīr.
rows.anchor: كان علي بن أبي طالب رضي الله عنه يقول

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says he is one of the few who know their number and affirms that they were seven and their dog was the eighth.
rows.anchor: وكان ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī's sixth argument is that God likely included the true count among the three reported counts; since the first two are conjecture, the third must be correct.
rows.anchor: فثبت أن جملة الأقوال الحقة والباطلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His seventh argument is that the Prophet was told not to dispute or consult them and that only a few know; the Prophet must have learned the correct count from revelation. The arguments together yield strength despite unequal force.
rows.anchor: فعلمنا أن العلم بهذه الواقعة حصل للنبي عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “they will say” omits “they” because the subject is clear from context.
rows.anchor: فحذف المبتدأ لدلالة الكلام عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The future particle appears before the first opinion, while conjunction carries the following two opinions into its scope.
rows.anchor: أن حرف العطف يوجب دخول القولين الآخرين فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rajm is throwing and ghayb is what is unseen; “guessing at the unseen” means speaking about what one does not truly know, without reflection.
rows.anchor: معناه أن يرى ما غاب عنه ولا يعرفه بالحقيقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A proposed “wāw of eight” says Arabs use seven for numerical abundance and mark the eighth with a waw of resumption; al-Qaffāl objects that the eighth descriptor in 59:23 has no waw.
rows.anchor: والناس يسمون هذه الواو واو الثمانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God, or those He informs, knows the detailed events of past and future; Ibn ʿAbbās claims to be one of the few, while al-Qāḍī says that claim is sound only if the Prophet informed him. Rāzī finds the combined evidence probabilistic, not conclusive.
rows.anchor: العلم بتفاصيل كائنات العالم والحوادث التي حدثت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Do not argue over the precise count: say there is no evidence for their count and suspend judgment; the verse parallels the command to debate People of the Book graciously.
rows.anchor: أن لا يكذبهم في تعيين ذلك العدد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the other disputants lack knowledge, the Prophet is also told not to ask them about the sleepers.
rows.anchor: ليس عندهم علم في هذا الباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opponents of analogical reasoning cite “guessing at the unseen” as proof that conjecture is blameworthy and that issuing a legal opinion based on conjecture is forbidden; a line glossed by al-Kashshāf uses rajm for what is merely supposed.
rows.anchor: نفاة القياس تمسكوا بهذه الآية

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf's cited line “it is not a report about her that is conjectured” uses marjum to mean supposed or conjectured.
rows.anchor: أي المظنون هكذا قاله صاحب الكشاف

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Commentators say the Prophet promised to answer three questions the next day without saying “if God wills”; revelation was delayed fifteen days, or forty in another report, before this verse came.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون إن القوم لما سألوا النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن المسائل الثلاثة

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qāḍī objects that the Prophet knew he could die or be impeded before tomorrow, so an unqualified promise risked a false statement and repelling people from him.
rows.anchor: كان عالما بأنه إذا أخبر عن أنه سيفعل الفعل الفلاني غدا فربما جاءته الوفاة

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qāḍī also objects that the verse contains many rules and benefits, so it should not be restricted to one occasion; Rāzī replies that multiple benefits do not rule out a single occasion.
rows.anchor: أن اشتماله على الفوائد الكثيرة لا يمنع من أن يكون سبب نزوله واحدا منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī answers that saying “if God wills” is preferable, but the Prophet may have forgotten it, which would be omission of what is better rather than wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: إلا أنه ربما اتفق له أنه نسي هذا الكلام لسبب من الأسباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading supplies “unless God permits you to make that statement,” so a person should not announce a future action without divine permission to say so.
rows.anchor: أن يأذن لك في ذلك القول ، والمعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading supplies the words “unless you say: if God wills”; this protects a promise from being a lie if death or another obstacle prevents its fulfillment.
rows.anchor: إلا أن تقول : { إن شاء الله } والسبب في أنه لا بد

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazila say God wills faith and obedience, but servants will unbelief and sin, so the servants' will overcomes God's.
rows.anchor: مذهب المعتزلة أن الله تعالى يريد الإيمان والطاعة من العبد والعبد يريد الكفر والمعصية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī's school holds that everything God wills occurs, including faith or unbelief; divine will overcomes the servant's will.
rows.anchor: فكل ما أراد الله تعالى فهو واقع فهو تعالى يريد الكفر من الكافر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “if God wills” qualification removes a false promise only if God's will can override the servant's will; a defeated divine will cannot excuse failure.
rows.anchor: فإن على هذا القول يكون التقدير أن العبد قال أنا أفعل الفعل الفلاني إلا إذا كانت إرادة الله بخلافه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The community agrees that adding “if God wills” to an oath prevents breach; Rāzī argues this proves God's will prevails and only what God wills comes to be.
rows.anchor: أجمعت الأمة على أنه إذا قال والله لأفعلن كذا ثم قال : إن شاء الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If a debtor swears to repay tomorrow and adds “if God wills,” failure does not break the oath even though repayment is commanded; thus God may command without willing and prohibit while willing.
rows.anchor: فإذا جاء الغد ولم يقض هذا الدين لم يحنث

rows.speaker: الفقهاء
rows.claim: Some jurists say conditional divorce does not take effect if the husband says “if God wills”; Rāzī explains that proving God's will would otherwise depend circularly on proving the divorce, and vice versa.
rows.anchor: إذا قال الرجل لامرأته أنت طالق إن شاء الله لم يقع الطلاق

rows.speaker: القائلون بأن المعدوم شيء
rows.claim: Those who say nonexistent things are things argue that a future action, now nonexistent, is called “a thing” in the verse; Rāzī replies that what will become a thing may be named so in advance, as in 16:1.
rows.anchor: الشيء الذي سيفعله الفاعل غدا سماه الله تعالى في الحال بأنه شيء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says that if a person forgets to qualify a promise and remembers much later, saying “if God wills” then still suffices to prevent oath-breaking.
rows.anchor: لو لم يحصل التذكر إلا بعد مدة طويلة ثم ذكر إن شاء الله كفى في دفع الحنث

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr permits the delayed qualification after a year, month, week, or day.
rows.anchor: وعن سعيد بن جبير بعد سنة أو شهر أو أسبوع أو يوم

rows.speaker: طاوس
rows.claim: Ṭāwūs allows the qualification only while the person remains in the same sitting.
rows.anchor: وعن طاوس أنه يقدر على الاستثناء في مجلسه

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ allows the qualification for roughly the time it takes to milk a plentifully yielding camel.
rows.anchor: وعن عطاء يستثني على مقدار حلب الناقة الغزيرة

rows.speaker: عامة الفقهاء
rows.claim: The majority of jurists say the qualification has no legal effect unless it is joined to the original statement.
rows.anchor: وعند عامة الفقهاء أنه لا أثر له في الأحكام ما لم يكن موصولا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās argues that the command to remember God when one forgets is not limited to a particular time, supporting a later qualification when one remembers.
rows.anchor: هو الذي تقدم ذكره في قوله : { إلا أن يشاء الله }

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa warns al-Manṣūr that allowing delayed qualifications would let people leave a pledge and later undo their oaths; al-Manṣūr approved the argument.
rows.anchor: فقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله : هذا يرجع عليك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says the jurists' appeal to settled contracts is a weak restriction of the text by analogy; a whispered qualification also avoids the stated public-doubt objection while counting by agreement.
rows.anchor: فثبت أن الذي عولوا عليه ليس بقوي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stronger case for requiring a connected qualification comes from commands to fulfill contracts and covenants: joined exception and statement form one utterance, while an unqualified, complete promise creates an obligation.
rows.anchor: الأولى أن يحتجوا في وجوب كون الاستثناء متصلا بأن الآيات الكثيرة دلت على وجوب الوفاء بالعقد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other glosses take remembering the Lord as praising and seeking forgiveness after forgetting the qualification, asking God to remind one of what was forgotten, or performing a missed prayer upon remembering.
rows.anchor: واذكر ربك بالتسبيح والاستغفار إذا نسيت كلمة الاستثناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī finds those readings remote: connecting the command to the previous discussion completes the argument, while treating it as a new topic breaks the discourse.
rows.anchor: وذكره أحسن من تركه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One gloss of “closer guidance” is that saying “if God wills” is better than omitting it.
rows.anchor: وذكره أحسن من تركه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another gloss is that God may guide the Prophet to something better or more complete than the promised answer.
rows.anchor: فيقول عسى أن يهديني ربي لشيء أحسن وأكمل مما وعدتكم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third gloss points to the cave story: God may grant stronger evidence for the Prophet's mission, as He later did through prophetic accounts and reports of the unseen.
rows.anchor: أن هذا حكاية كلام القوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take the statement that the youths stayed 300 years as a quotation of what people say, supported by the reply that follows and a reading in ʿAbd Allāh's codex, “and they said.”
rows.anchor: هو كلام الله تعالى فإنه أخبر عن كمية تلك المدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others take the 300-year statement as God's own report; the intervening prohibition of disputation separates it from the earlier quoted claims, and the reply directs people to God's knowledge rather than the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: هو كلام الله تعالى فإنه أخبر

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read thalāth miʾat sinīn without tanwīn; the others use tanwīn. With tanwīn, sinīn is apposition explaining the unit, or the order is inverted to “years, three hundred.”
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة والكسائي ثلثمائة سنين بغير تنوين والباقون بالتنوين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Under Ḥamza's reading, the normal construct would be “three hundred years,” but plural can stand in a specification where singular is expected, as in 18:103.
rows.anchor: الواجب في الإضافة ثلثمائة سنة إلا أنه يجوز وضع الجمع موضع الواحد في التمييز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says 300 solar years equal 309 lunar years, though Rāzī says the arithmetic does not support it.
rows.anchor: كانت المدة ثلثمائة سنة من السنين الشمسية وثلثمائة وتسع سنين من القمرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī tentatively suggests that after completing 300 years, circumstances may have prolonged their sleep by nine more years.
rows.anchor: لعلهم لما استكملوا ثلثمائة سنة قرب أمرهم من الأنبياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows the duration better than disputing people because He created the heavens and earth and governs the world, so He necessarily knows its unseen events.
rows.anchor: وإنما كان أولى بأن يكون عالما به لأنه موجد للسموات والأرض ومدبر للعالم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “How seeing and hearing He is” is an Arabic expression of wonder, discussed also in the commentary on 2:175.
rows.anchor: كلمة تذكر في التعجب ، والمعنى ما أبصره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They have no protector besides Him” may mean God alone preserved the sleepers; that disputants need His care and cannot know without His informing them; or that no protector can shield those who defy His report from punishment.
rows.anchor: ما لأصحاب الكهف من دون الله من ولي فإنه هو الذي يتولى حفظهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one shares God's judgment: a partner could object and impede the other, as in the argument that multiple gods would bring disorder.
rows.anchor: والأصل أن الاثنين إذا كانا لشريكين فإن الاعتراض من كل واحد منهما على صاحبه يكثر

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir reads lā tushrik with second-person tāʾ and jussive, attaching the prohibition to “do not say” or “remember your Lord”; it means do not consult anyone about their number or seek another's knowledge.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر ولا تشرك بالتاء والجزم على النهي والخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The other readers use third-person yaʾ with indicative mood, stating that God does not share His judgment.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الباقون بالياء والرفع على الخبر والمعنى أنه تعالى لا يفعل ذلك
